confirmed.title: Every semantic color token is undefined — errors, successes, and warnings all render as the same neutral gray
confirmed.detail:
Both themes in web/src/app.css define only base/primary/secondary/neutral. They define no --color-error, --color-success, --color-warning, --color-info (verified: `grep '--color-error:' dist/assets/*.css` returns nothing). DaisyUI's `.alert-error{--alert-color:var(--color-error)}` therefore computes to guaranteed-invalid, the `var(--alert-color, var(--color-base-200))` fallback fires, and every alert paints base-200 — the exact same fill as the SpecCard sitting above it. Same for `.badge-success/-error/-warning` and `.step-success/-error`.

Proven three ways: (a) the built rejected capture — "Couldn't add this album" is a flat gray box with a hairline border, visually identical to the format panel; (b) the history capture — "wrong format", "needs a look", and "in library" chips are all the same gray, and the *failure* chip is the least visible of the three; (c) a probe page against the built CSS (dist/assets/index-IQcOmWuR.css) rendering alert-error / alert-warning / alert-success / all four badges — every one came out identical gray.

The step spine is the worst symptom: in the built capture, steps 1 (step-success ✓) and 2 (step-error !) have NO marker disc at all — the glyphs float bare on the connector line — while steps 3 and 4 ('upcoming', no color class, so they get the real base-300 default) show solid discs. The completed and failed steps are less visible than the ones that haven't happened. A family member looks at that spine and reads the failure as the least important thing on it.

The repo's own contract says reject wording is load-bearing. Shipping it in the same gray as a success chip breaks that contract visually.
confirmed.fix: Add --color-error / -success / -warning / -info (and their -content pairs) to BOTH theme blocks, sourced from Navidrome's MUI palette the same way the base colors were. Then re-verify the step spine and the badge row — those two are the proof surfaces.
confirmed.verifier_reasoning:
CONFIRMED — I could not refute any part of this finding; every claim checks out against the actual code and the actual built captures.

**1. The tokens are genuinely absent.** `/var/home/glw907/Projects/dubplate/web/src/app.css` has exactly two `@plugin 'daisyui/theme'` blocks (navidrome-light at line ~16, navidrome-dark at ~30). Each defines only ten tokens: base-100/200/300/base-content, primary/-content, secondary/-content, neutral/-content. No error, success, warning, info, or accent — and no `-content` pairs for them.

I checked whether DaisyUI backfills defaults, which would have refuted the finding. It does not. `web/node_modules/daisyui/theme/index.js` merges built-in defaults only under `if (allThemes[name])` — i.e. only when the theme name matches a shipped DaisyUI theme. `navidrome-light` / `navidrome-dark` are not built-ins, so `themeTokens` is exactly what the block declared. The built CSS proves it: the emitted `:root),[data-theme=navidrome-light]{…}` rule contains precisely those ten custom properties and stops. `grep -o '\-\-color-error:[^;]*;' web/dist/assets/index-IQcOmWuR.css` returns nothing, likewise `--color-success:` and `--color-warning:`. I also grepped `web/src/`, `web/index.html`, and `internal/serve/` for any other definition site — nothing.

**2. The consuming rules exist and are used.** The built CSS does emit `.alert-error{color:var(--color-error-content);--alert-border-color:var(--color-error);--alert-color:var(--color-error)}` (and -info/-success/-warning), `.badge-error{--badge-color:var(--color-error);--badge-fg:var(--color-error-content)}` (and -success/-warning), and `.steps .step-error+.step-error:before,.steps .step-error:after,.steps .step-error>.step-icon{--step-bg:var(--color-error);--step-fg:var(--color-error-content)}` (and -success/-warning/-info). The base rules fall back: `.alert{background-color:var(--alert-color,var(--color-base-200))}`, `.alert{border-color:var(--alert-border-color,var(--color-base-200))}`, `.badge{border:… var(--badge-color,var(--color-base-200));--badge-bg:var(--badge-color,var(--color-base-100))}`.

Those classes are live in eleven source sites: `App.svelte:356,404,458`, `lib/components/Journey.svelte:190,219`, `lib/components/OutcomeAlert.svelte:33,55,64,73`, `lib/components/History.svelte:77,79,85`, `lib/components/FileRow.svelte:58`, `lib/components/JourneySteps.svelte:46,50`. This is not a dormant rule — it is the entire outcome and verdict surface.

The CSS mechanism is exactly as described: a custom property whose value fails var() substitution computes to the guaranteed-invalid value, so a later `var(--alert-color, fallback)` takes the fallback (base-200), while non-custom properties like `color:var(--color-error-content)` become invalid-at-computed-value-time and reset to inherit. Result: alert-error, alert-warning, alert-success, and alert-info all paint an identical base-200 fill with a base-200 border and inherited text color.

**3. All three of the reviewer's visual proofs hold in the built captures.** I read both JPGs myself rather than trusting the description.

`rejected-journey-desktop-1440.jpg`: the "Couldn't add this album" alert is a flat gray panel with a hairline border, the same fill as the FLAC spec card directly above it. Nothing on the page reads as a failure.

The step spine in that same capture is the sharpest symptom and is exactly as claimed. Steps 1 (✓, step-success) and 2 (!, step-error) have **no marker disc at all** — the glyphs sit bare on the connector line, because `.step-icon`'s `background-color:var(--step-bg)` is invalid (transparent) and its `border:1px solid var(--step-bg)` shorthand drops to `border-style:none`. Steps 3 and 4 carry no color class, so they keep the real `--step-bg:var(--color-base-300)` default and render as solid discs. The finished and the failed steps are visibly less present than the two that have not happened yet.

`history-desktop-1440.jpg`: "wrong format" (badge-error) has **no chip fill whatsoever** — it reads as bare text; "needs a look" (badge-warning) and "in library" (badge-success) both show the same faint gray chip. The failure state is the least visible of the three, and the failure and success chips are indistinguishable from each other.

**4. It breaks a stated repo contract.** CLAUDE.md: "Reject wording is contract (`internal/reject` / `friendly_reason`): the uploader page and emails share it verbatim." Rendering that wording in the identical gray as a success chip — and rendering the failure step of the journey spine as the least visible marker on it — defeats the contract at the presentation layer.

Scope note beyond the original finding: `alert-info` is also used (`OutcomeAlert.svelte:64`, the private-recordings / informational outcome), so `--color-info` and `--color-info-content` are needed too, not just error/success/warning. `--color-accent` is likewise undefined but no source uses `*-accent`, so it is optional.

The proposed fix is right, and the two named proof surfaces (step spine, history badge row) are the correct re-verification targets. Severity blocker is appropriate.

confirmed.title: DaisyUI 5 `.alert` is display:grid, so `flex-col items-start` is inert — every multi-paragraph alert lays out as newspaper columns
confirmed.detail:
`.alert` in daisyui 5.7.25 is `display:grid; grid-auto-flow:column; place-items:center start` (confirmed in node_modules/daisyui/components/alert.css and in the built dist CSS). `flex-col` and `items-start` are flexbox properties and do nothing to a grid container. Every alert in the app carries exactly that combination.

The built rejected capture already shows it: "Couldn't add this album" and "The album didn't pass its checks." sit side by side on one line, not stacked.

The pushed-back alert is where it becomes an embarrassment. I rendered it against the built CSS: heading, paragraph 1, paragraph 2, and the three-button div become FOUR grid columns. The main explanatory paragraph is squeezed into a ~70px column reading "MusicBrainz / didn't find a / match for / this album," — one or two words per line, twenty lines tall. This is the primary recovery screen (contract section 5B); it is unreadable.

Affected: App.svelte:356 (signed-out), :404 (preflight-rejected), :458 (upload stopped); OutcomeAlert.svelte:33, :55, :64, :73 (all four outcomes); Journey.svelte:190 (in-library), :219 (format-rejected).
confirmed.fix: Replace `flex-col items-start` with DaisyUI's own `alert-vertical` (grid-auto-flow:row) plus `text-left`/`justify-items:start`, or drop `.alert` grid layout by wrapping the children in a single child div. Fix all nine sites; a unit assertion on computed grid-auto-flow would keep it fixed.
confirmed.verifier_reasoning:

2. Override hunt — none exists. `grep` for any rule matching `*alert*{...display:flex...}` in the built CSS returns nothing. `grep -rn "<style" web/src/` returns nothing at all: the app has zero Svelte scoped styles. `alert-vertical`/`alert-horizontal` appear nowhere in `web/src/` (and consequently `.alert-vertical{` is absent from the built CSS entirely, tree-shaken as unused). Nothing rescues the layout.

3. Existing capture — the finding's read of `/var/home/glw907/.claude/jobs/daef7196/tmp/captures/rejected-journey-desktop-1440.jpg` is correct. "Couldn't add this album" and "The album didn't pass its checks." render side by side on one baseline, two grid columns, not stacked. This is a real capture of the real binary, not a reconstruction.

4. Blocker severity is right. Every alert in the app is affected, including the primary recovery screen and the reject-wording contract screen.

The team clearly knows the rule — CollectionPicker's select (line 44) and every AlbumCard input carry an explicit `min-h-11`. The buttons were just missed. AlbumCard is the clearest tell: 44px inputs stacked directly above a 40px submit.

confirmed.title: The light theme ships undesigned and unreviewed — badges disappear entirely and errors are white on white

confirmed.title: Store session state is never reset between uploads: a second album can finish and poll the FIRST album's session ID
confirmed.detail:
`UploadStore.session` (upload.svelte.ts:358) is written in exactly one place — `createSession` — and is never cleared. `App.resetSelection()` (App.svelte:170-178) resets `phase`/`pendingFiles`/`preflightRejections` and nothing else. `journeySessionId` is `$derived.by(() => uploadStore.session.sessionId ? uploadStore.session.sessionId : sessionIdFromUploadURL(currentFiles[0].tusUploadURL))` — the store's session ID unconditionally wins.

Reachable path: upload album A as a multi-file selection (`createSession` sets `session.sessionId = A`) → A is pushed back → user clicks "Fix the names and retry" (`onFixNames = resetSelection`) → user picks album B as a single .zip → `beginUpload` takes the ZIP branch (App.svelte:146-151) which deliberately never calls `createSession` → `session.sessionId` is still A → `journeySessionId` returns A. `Journey` then POSTs `/api/session/A/finish` and polls `/api/journey/A` for album B's upload, and `journeyAlbum` (App.svelte:216, `uploadStore.session.album || ...`) shows album A's title. The family member watches album B's upload complete and is told album A is in their library.

The same root cause hits `handleResumeFilesPicked` (App.svelte:277-282): it starts the resumed files against `row.sessionId` but `journeySessionId` still prefers the stale `session.sessionId`, and `retryStalled` (App.svelte:238) builds `session_id` metadata from `uploadStore.session.sessionId ?? journeySessionId ?? ''`, so a stalled retry can be tagged with the wrong session too.

`uploadStore.journey` and `uploadStore.journeyOutcome` have the identical problem: `Journey.viewMode` reads `journey?.state` as soon as its own `outcome` resolves, so a stale `journey.state === 'in-library'` from album A renders the "In your library" success card (with A's `libraryLink`) for album B before B's first poll returns.

Call it from `App.resetSelection()` and at the top of `beginUpload()` (before the branch), and also from `handleResumeFilesPicked` before adopting `row.sessionId`. Separately, make `journeySessionId` prefer an explicitly-tracked session for the current selection rather than falling back to a store field that outlives it — e.g. hold a local `let currentSessionId = $state<string | null>(null)` in App.svelte, set it in `beginUpload`/`handleResumeFilesPicked`, and derive from that with the ZIP URL parse as the only fallback.

confirmed.title: "Upload to Private Recordings" from History leads to an empty tag form and a zero-file upload
confirmed.detail:
`App.svelte:346-349` wires History's `onUploadPrivate` to `retryAsPrivateCollection()`. That function (App.svelte:219-231) derives the tag form's rows from `pendingFiles`, the in-memory selection from the *current* session. A History row is by definition a past session — after a reload `pendingFiles` is `[]`, and even without one it holds whatever the user last picked, not the row's files.

So the path renders `AlbumCard` with zero track rows, and `submitTagForm` -> `beginUpload([])` -> `createSession(album, collection, 0)` with an empty `uploadFileIds`. `allFilesLanded` requires `currentFiles.length > 0`, so `Journey` never mounts either: the user lands on a permanently blank uploading phase with no error, no progress, and no way back except the masthead toggle. This is reachable by expanding any pushed-back row in "Your uploads" and pressing the primary action — the single most likely recovery path a family member takes.

Outside strict a11y scope, but it breaks the "whole journey operable" criterion and would embarrass in front of a user.
confirmed.fix: Route History's pushed-back re-upload through the same re-pick flow `handleResume` uses (open a scoped picker, then tag), or disable/hide the "Upload to Private Recordings" action inside the History disclosure and leave only "Fix the names and retry", which correctly resets to the idle picker. At minimum, guard `retryAsPrivateCollection` with `if (pendingFiles.length === 0) return;` plus a live-region message, so the flow never dead-ends silently.

confirmed.title: GET /api/journey/{id} mutates another user's session state and emails the admin before it checks ownership
confirmed.detail:
`handleJourney` calls `j.advance(r.Context(), id, now)` at /var/home/glw907/Projects/dubplate/internal/serve/api.go:85, and only then builds the live set and calls `j.authorize(...)` at api.go:88-98. `advance` is not a read: it calls `journey.AdvanceInLibrary`, which appends a `ledger.StateInLibrary` event (internal/journey/journey.go:175-185), and then `journey.AdvanceStalled`, which appends a `ledger.StateStalled` event AND sends mail to the admin (journey.go:131-148).

Attack: Bob is on the roster (any family member). He learns or is shown Alice's 26-char session ID — from a shared screenshot, a copied URL, an admin mail subject that literally contains `Session %s ... contributor %s`, or an inbox directory name `<sessionid>__<album>`. Bob GETs `/upload/api/journey/<alice-id>`. He receives a 404 and learns nothing from the body, but the server has already:
  1. appended a `stalled` event to Alice's session if her latest event is older than `StallMinutes`, which is the de-dupe record, so it permanently suppresses the real stall notification that would have fired later; and
  2. sent the admin an email titled "dubplate: alice@…'s upload has stalled".
That is unauthenticated-relative-to-the-resource state mutation plus notification forgery, triggerable at 5-second poll cadence.

It also defeats the no-existence-oracle property the surrounding comments claim (api.go:69-71, api.go:218-221). `advance` returns instantly when `len(events) == 0` (api.go:190-194) but makes an outbound Navidrome `getScanStatus` HTTP call (10s-bounded) when the session exists and is in `tagging`. The response-time difference between "this session ID exists in the ledger" and "it does not" is trivially measurable, and it is exactly the distinction the 404 shape was designed to hide.
confirmed.fix: Move the `advance` call below the authorization check: build `lb`, run `j.authorize(id, email, lb)`, 404 on failure, and only then `advance`. `authorize` already reads the ledger itself, so the reordering costs nothing.
confirmed.verifier_reasoning:
CONFIRMED — I could not refute the core mechanism; I reproduced it by execution.

Code reading (verbatim confirmation):
- /var/home/glw907/Projects/dubplate/internal/serve/api.go:84-98 — `now := j.deps.Now()`, then `j.advance(r.Context(), id, now)` on line 85, then `lb := j.buildLive(email)` (89) and `j.authorize(id, email, lb)` (90) with the 404 at 96. The ordering is exactly as the finding states.
- `advance` (api.go:185-212) is a writer, not a reader: it calls `journey.AdvanceInLibrary` (journey.go:158-186, appends `ledger.StateInLibrary`) and `journey.AdvanceStalled` (journey.go:122-149, appends `ledger.StateStalled` then `send(ctx, adminEmail, …)` with subject `dubplate: %s's upload has stalled` and a body naming the session ID, album, and contributor email).
- `authorize` (api.go:222-234) does its own `Ledger.Session(sessionID)` read, so the reorder the finding proposes genuinely costs nothing. I checked the owner-facing paths for regressions: a live-only session short-circuits `authorize` via `lb.set`, a ledger-owned session passes on `events[0].Email`, and `finish` only consumes `lb.details` in the `StateQueued` branch — so moving `advance` below the check changes nothing for a legitimate owner.

Empirical proof (temporary test in internal/serve, since run and removed; tree left clean): seeded one `queued` event for alice@example.com on session `alicegenericsessionxxxxxxx` dated 90 minutes before `now` with `StallMinutes: 30`, then issued Bob's `GET /api/journey/alicegenericsessionxxxxxxx`. Result: HTTP 404 to Bob, and Alice's ledger came back with two events, latest `stalled`. The mail path also fired — the handler logged `journey: advance session … err="notify admin of stalled session alicegenericsessionxxxxxxx: send to admin@example.com via 127.0.0.1:25: dial failed: connection refused"`, i.e. the send was attempted and only failed for want of an SMTP server in the test env. So both halves of the claim (foreign ledger write + admin mail before the ownership check) are real.

Scope checks that did not refute it: the requester must be Access-verified and on the roster (serve.go:279-305), and session IDs are 128 bits of crypto/rand base32 (session.go:27-40), so this needs a roster member who has been handed another member's ID rather than an outsider. `handleHistory` (api.go:151) calls the same `advance`, but only over IDs from `Ledger.History(email)` and the requester's own live set, so it is already ownership-scoped — the defect is confined to `handleJourney`.

Severity calibration, where I do think the write-up overreaches (worth trimming when the finding is folded, but not grounds for refuting it):
1. "Notification forgery" is too strong. `AdvanceStalled` gates on `now.Sub(latest.At) >= stallMinutes` (journey.go:127), so Bob can only trigger a *truthful* alert about a genuinely overdue session, and no earlier than the real stall deadline. He cannot manufacture an alert for a healthy session, and the same is true of the in-library promotion, which requires a real Navidrome scan completion after the tagging event.
2. "Permanently suppresses the real stall notification that would have fired later" is backwards as written — the notification is sent in the same call. There IS a suppression bug here, but it is a different one and not attacker-specific: `AdvanceStalled` appends the de-dupe event *before* it sends, with no rollback, so any single SMTP failure (exactly what my probe run hit) permanently swallows that session's stall notification. That deserves its own finding.
3. "Triggerable at 5-second poll cadence" overstates it. The mutation is one-shot: the appended `stalled` event is the de-dupe record (`hasState`, journey.go:124), and in-library is terminal, so repeated polls do nothing further.
4. The existence-oracle half is real but close to inert. The extra outbound `getScanStatus` call only happens while the latest event is `StateTagging`, and with unguessable 128-bit IDs the timing signal only helps someone who already holds a valid foreign ID — in which case they already know it exists.

Net: the defect is a genuine ordering bug — an unauthorized-relative-to-the-resource request performs a persistent ledger write and an outbound email on a stranger's session — and the one-line reorder fix is correct and free, so it should land. Its real-world impact is milder than the write-up's "forgery / suppression / 5-second cadence" framing suggests; I would file it as major on principle (state mutation ahead of the ownership check, in a handler whose own doc comments at api.go:69-71 and 218-221 claim the opposite property) rather than for the described attack payoff.

confirmed.title: Unvalidated tus upload ID reaches filepath.Join; percent-encoded traversal confirmed working end to end
confirmed.detail:
`enforceUploadOwnership` derives the upload ID as `id := strings.Trim(r.URL.Path, "/")` (/var/home/glw907/Projects/dubplate/internal/serve/upload.go:326) and hands it straight to `e.store.GetUpload(r.Context(), id)` (upload.go:338). tusd's `filestore` performs no ID validation whatsoever: `infoPath` is `filepath.Join(store.Path, id+".info")` and `defaultBinPath` is `filepath.Join(store.Path, id)` (filestore.go:195-202). tusd's own handlers use the identical `strings.Trim(path, "/")` extraction (handler/unrouted_handler.go:1678-1680), so whatever ID gets past this middleware is the ID tusd's HEAD/PATCH/DELETE act on.

Go's ServeMux only canonicalizes the *escaped* path, so `..%2f` survives every layer: `mountBasePath` matches on `r.URL.Path`, `http.StripPrefix` trims both `Path` and `RawPath`, and the middleware then reads the decoded `r.URL.Path`. Verified live against the dev binary on 127.0.0.1:8090. I planted a syntactically valid tusd `.info` file one directory above UploadsDir with `MetaData.email` set to the dev identity, then:

    files/zzprobe            404
    files/%2e%2e/zzprobe     404   (encoded dots, path stays multi-segment)
    files/..%2fzzprobe       200   <-- traversal succeeded
    files/%2e%2e%2fzzprobe   200   <-- traversal succeeded

The 200s mean `filepath.Join(UploadsDir, "../zzprobe.info")` was read, the ownership check passed on its metadata, and tusd's HeadFile served it. Probe file removed afterwards.

Honest exploitability bound: to weaponize this an attacker needs a file at a traversable path that (a) ends in `.info`, (b) parses as tusd `handler.FileInfo` JSON, and (c) carries their own verified email in `MetaData`. They cannot plant one, because `preCreate` overrides `changes.ID` with the server-chosen `sess.ID + "-" + slot` (upload.go:430-437). So this is a latent traversal rather than a live read/write primitive today. It is still a real defect: the app validates session IDs with `validSessionID` at every other ingress (upload.go:383, upload.go:909, api.go:79, serve.go:535) and skips validation on the one path that feeds an unguarded `filepath.Join`, leaving the whole chain one tusd or config change away from arbitrary-path reads and DELETEs.
confirmed.fix: In `enforceUploadOwnership`, validate the ID against the shape `preCreate` actually mints before touching the store: `^[a-z2-7]{26}-[0-9]+$`. Anything else gets `http.NotFound`, consistent with the existing no-oracle 404 shape. This is the same discipline `validSessionID` already applies everywhere else.

The only guards in `enforceUploadOwnership` are `id == ""` (pass-through for the bare create) and the metadata email match.

confirmed.title: Completed sessions are never removed from the store and never swept from disk: unbounded memory and disk growth
confirmed.detail:
`Engine.completeSession` runs a session to a terminal outcome and returns, but never calls `e.sessions.delete(sess.ID)` (/var/home/glw907/Projects/dubplate/internal/serve/upload.go:625-663). The only deleter is `SweepOnce` (upload.go:768-776), which targets `e.sessions.expired(cutoff)` — and `expired` explicitly filters to `!done && sess.createdAt.Before(cutoff)` (internal/serve/session.go:330-334). A completed session is therefore permanently resident in the `Store` map, holding its `verdicts` slice.

Disk is worse. Trace each terminal branch:
  - format verdict fails -> `e.discard(sess)` removes the dir (upload.go:637). Memory leaks, disk is fine.
  - private lane / confident match -> `promote` renames the dir into the inbox. Memory leaks, disk is fine.
  - `PushedBack` (unconfident tag match) -> dir deliberately left under UploadsDir (upload.go:656-657).
  - `ProbeUnavailable` -> dir deliberately left under UploadsDir (upload.go:652-654).
  - `promoteInto` rename failure -> dir deliberately left in place (upload.go:672-677).
None of the last three is ever reclaimed by anything: not the sweep (session is `completed`), not a systemd timer (nothing in systemd/ or scripts/deploy.sh touches /srv/music/uploads), not a `dubplate` subcommand. Every pushed-back album accumulates full-size FLAC content forever.

The failure mode is a slow lockout: `preCreate` rejects with `ReasonNoSpace` once `avail - Size < FreeFloorGB` (upload.go:421-428). With the default 5 GiB floor and a family sending lossless albums, a handful of pushed-back uploads is enough. Combined with the TagProbe blocker above, *every* main-lane upload currently lands in this bucket.
confirmed.fix: Two changes. (1) Give the sweep a second cutoff for settled sessions: sweep a completed session's store entry after a short grace (long enough for the journey poll to read the outcome back), so the map does not grow without bound. (2) Give `PushedBack` / `ProbeUnavailable` / failed-promote directories an explicit retention TTL and reclaim them on the same ticker, or move them to a reviewable holding directory an operator sees, rather than leaving them where the free-space admission check will eventually trip over them.

CONFIRMED. Every cited line reads exactly as the finding describes, and an exhaustive search for a counter-mechanism found none.

Verified point by point:

1. `Engine.completeSession` (internal/serve/upload.go:625-663) has four `return` paths and none calls `e.sessions.delete`. Confirmed by reading the whole function.

2. `Session.completeOnce` (internal/serve/session.go:184-193) sets `sess.completed = true` at the *top* of `completeSession`, before any outcome is decided. So the session is `done` from the first instant of completion.

3. `Store.expired` (session.go:324-336) filters `if !done && sess.createdAt.Before(cutoff)`. A completed session can therefore never appear in the sweep's target list.

4. `grep -rn "\.delete(" internal/serve/*.go` (excluding tests) returns exactly ONE call site: `internal/serve/upload.go:773`, inside `SweepOnce`, iterating `e.sessions.expired(cutoff)`. There is no other deleter anywhere in the package. The map genuinely grows monotonically for the process lifetime.

5. Disk: `grep -rn "RemoveAll"` across internal/, scripts/, systemd/, cmd/ shows only two functions ever remove a path under `UploadsDir` — `discard` (upload.go:755, reached only on `!verdict.OK`) and `sweepOne` (upload.go:778, reached only for non-completed sessions). `assembleUpload`'s `os.RemoveAll(sessionDir)` at upload.go:571 is an assembly-failure path, not a reclaim. The `PushedBack` (656), `ProbeUnavailable` (653), and failed-`promoteInto` (672-677) directories are touched by nothing.

6. No external reclaim exists. `systemd/` contains backup, disk-check, import, navidrome-check, import-nudge, serve, ping-fail — nothing sweeping uploads; `dubplate-disk-check` only alerts. The only tmpfiles.d fragment (`config/tmpfiles-dubplate.conf`, installed at deploy.sh:229) covers `/run/dubplate/nudge-triggers`, with no age-based cleanup on `/srv/music/uploads`. deploy.sh:362-378 only `mkdir -p`s the directory. `internal/importer` never references `UploadsDir` (it scans InboxDir); `internal/review` operates on the review root. No `dubplate` subcommand touches it (`cmd/dubplate` references UploadsDir only in `doctor.go`'s read/write probe).

7. The lockout mechanism checks out: upload.go:421-427 computes `floor := int64(e.cfg.Thresholds.FreeFloorGB) * bytesPerGiB` and returns `reject.ReasonNoSpace` with 507. `defaultFreeFloorGB = 5` (config.go:153) and `defaultPartialTTL = 24h` (config.go:180) confirm the defaults quoted.

One thing the finding UNDERSTATES, found while verifying: the serve Engine writes no `ledger` event at all (the only ledger use in serve is read-side, in `api.go`; `serve.go:134` wires `OnPromoted` solely to `writeNudgeTrigger`). So a pushed-back album's *only* record anywhere is the orphaned directory plus the in-memory Store entry — it is invisible to `/api/history` after a restart and unreclaimable by an operator who does not go looking on the box by hand.

- The memory half alone is minor: a `Session` plus its verdict slice is small, and a process restart clears the map. The disk half is what makes this major.
- The proposed "sweep completed sessions after a grace" needs care: `sessionOutcome.Detail` (the pushed-back reason) lives ONLY in the in-memory Store, since nothing persists it. Deleting the entry would silently drop the pushed-back detail from the journey/history UI unless a ledger event is written first.

confirmed.title: The partial-upload sweep is memory-only, so any serve restart permanently orphans staged directories and breaks tus resume
confirmed.detail:
`SweepOnce` finds its targets by iterating the in-process `Store` map (/var/home/glw907/Projects/dubplate/internal/serve/upload.go:768-776 and internal/serve/session.go:324-337). It never scans UploadsDir. The `Store` is plain in-memory state with no persistence (session.go:244-252).

So on every `systemd restart dubplate-serve` — a deploy, a crash, `Restart=` firing — the entire session map is discarded while the on-disk artifacts survive: assembled session directories `<UploadsDir>/<sessionid>/`, raw tus blobs `<UploadsDir>/<sessionid>-<slot>`, and their `.info` sidecars. Nothing will ever delete them. `PartialTTL` (24h default) becomes decorative: it only ages out sessions the process still remembers.

The contributor-facing half is worse than the disk half. After a restart, a resuming tus client's PATCH passes `enforceUploadOwnership` (the `.info` file still carries their email), reaches `preFinish`, and hits `e.sessions.get(sessionID)` returning not-found -> `fmt.Errorf("serve: session %s vanished before finish", ...)` -> a 500 (upload.go:450-454). The whole point of tus here is resumable uploads over a family member's phone connection, and the web store surfaces `resumable` history rows; a routine deploy silently converts every in-flight resumable upload into a hard failure with an internal-sounding error.
confirmed.fix: Make the sweep filesystem-driven rather than map-driven: at each tick (and once at startup), stat every entry under UploadsDir and remove anything older than `PartialTTL` that the live map does not claim. That reclaims restart orphans and is the only version of the sweep that is correct across a restart. For resume specifically, either persist minimal session metadata (the sidecar shape is already defined) or reconstruct the session from the surviving `.info` metadata in `preFinish` instead of 500-ing.
confirmed.verifier_reasoning:
CONFIRMED — I tried to refute this on four independent fronts and every one closed against refutation.

1. The sweep really is map-only. `SweepOnce` (internal/serve/upload.go:768-776) gets its target list solely from `e.sessions.expired(cutoff)`, and `Store.expired` (session.go:324-337) ranges the in-memory `s.sessions` map. `Store` is `map[string]*Session` behind a mutex with no load/save path (session.go:244-251). I grepped all of internal/serve for filesystem enumeration: the only `ReadDir`/`Walk`/`Glob` in the non-test package code is `filepath.Glob` inside `sweepOne` (upload.go:784), and it is already scoped to `sess.ID+"-*"` for a session the map handed it. Nothing ever enumerates UploadsDir.

2. Nothing outside the process reclaims it either. UploadsDir is `/srv/music/uploads` (scripts/deploy.sh:375-377), plain persistent disk; deploy.sh only `mkdir -p && chown`, never cleans. config/tmpfiles-dubplate.conf covers only `/run/dubplate` and `/run/dubplate/nudge-triggers`, deliberately per its own comment. No systemd unit touches uploads (the only `uploads` hits under systemd/ are a Description line, the ReadWritePaths entry, and an unrelated R2 comment in the backup timer). There is no startup purge: `Server.Run` (serve.go:604-621) starts listeners and `RunSweep`, nothing else. So an orphaned `<UploadsDir>/<sessionid>/` directory, plus every `<sessionid>-<slot>` blob and its `.info` sidecar, survives forever after a restart, and `PartialTTL` is decorative against them. Those blobs also permanently consume the free-space budget `preCreate` admits against (upload.go:421-428).

3. The resume-500 half is real end to end, and I traced it rather than assuming it. On a resume PATCH, `enforceUploadOwnership` (upload.go:324-359) passes: it reads ownership from the surviving `.info` via `e.store.GetUpload`, and its `e.sessions.get(...)` call only sets an optional `Upload-Expires` header, so a miss is silently tolerated (lines 353-355) and nothing stops the request. tusd then writes bytes and, at declared size, fires `PreFinishResponseCallback` -> `preFinish` (upload.go:449-454), whose `e.sessions.get(sessionID)` misses and returns a bare error. I read tusd v2.10.0 to confirm the status rather than guess: `emitFinishEvents` propagates the error (unrouted_handler.go:1003-1010) and `sendError` (unrouted_handler.go:1272-1280) wraps any non-`handler.Error` as `ERR_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` / HTTP 500 with `err.Error()` as the message.

4. Resume across a restart is a designed, exercised path, not a theoretical one. web/src/lib/store/upload.svelte.ts persists `ResumeAnchor` records (fileId, name, size, tusUploadURL) to `localStorage` under `dubplate:upload:resume-anchors` (lines 248-283, 473-474), hydrates them at construction (`hydrateResumeAnchors`, lines 383/695), replays them through `resumeURL` on `startFile` (line 469), and History.svelte renders a literal `· resume` affordance for such rows (History.svelte:71, 111). Crucially the resumed upload reuses the OLD tus resource, whose stored `.info` metadata still carries the dead `session_id`; re-creating a session client-side cannot repair that. Every such resume after a restart is guaranteed to fail at the finish.

Two refinements to the finding's wording, neither of which changes the severity:

confirmed.title: No CSRF defense on any state-changing POST: /api/session accepts a CORS-simple cross-origin request
confirmed.detail:
Nothing in `internal/serve/` inspects `Origin`, `Referer`, or `Sec-Fetch-Site`, and `handleCreateSession` decodes the body without checking `Content-Type` (/var/home/glw907/Projects/dubplate/internal/serve/upload.go:877-881). Verified live against the dev binary:

    curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: text/plain' -H 'Origin: https://evil.example' \
         --data '{"album":"csrf test","collection":"","expected_files":1}' \
         http://127.0.0.1:8090/upload/api/session
    -> HTTP/1.1 201 Created  {"session_id":"srum5ssgaxtxkdz5xlmv5zbpim"}

`text/plain` + no custom headers is precisely the shape a cross-origin `<form>` or `fetch` can send with no preflight, so nothing in the browser stops it reaching the origin. `POST /api/stream/probe` has the same property.

Concrete impact if the request carries credentials: `MaxSessionsPerUser` is 3 and `PartialTTL` is 24h (internal/config/config.go:180-181). Three cross-site POSTs from a page a family member visits exhaust their entire session quota, and `countActive` counts non-completed sessions, so `preCreate` and `handleCreateSession` both start answering `ReasonTooManySessions` for a full day. The victim cannot upload and has no way to clear it.

Whether the browser attaches the credential is not this code's decision to leave to chance: the Access `CF_Authorization` cookie's `SameSite` attribute is a Zero Trust application setting, and cloudflared injects `Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion` from whatever cookie arrives. The tus surface is incidentally protected (`Tus-Resumable`/`Upload-Length` force a preflight, and tusd's default CORS config is `AllowOrigin: .*` with `AllowCredentials: false`), but `/api/session` and `/api/stream/probe` are not.
confirmed.fix: Add one middleware in front of the mux that rejects any non-GET/HEAD whose `Origin` (falling back to `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`) does not match the configured public origin, and require `Content-Type: application/json` on the JSON POSTs. Do not rely on the Access cookie's SameSite value. See the OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet's "Verifying Origin With Standard Headers" section; Cloudflare's Zero Trust docs cover the cookie settings that determine whether the credential rides along at all.

2. `handleCreateSession` accepts any Content-Type — CONFIRMED.

  POST /upload/api/session, `Content-Type: text/plain`, `Origin: https://evil.example`
  -> `HTTP/1.1 201 Created  {"session_id":"nbbz3w36iea3jghsgr5xyrtgaq"}`

The reviewer correctly flagged that the `CF_Authorization` SameSite value is a Zero Trust app setting, and hedged on it.     HTTP/1.1 200 OK
    Accept-Ranges: bytes
    Cache-Control: no-cache
    Content-Length: 406
    Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

confirmed.title: POST /api/stream/probe is a gate-measurement endpoint shipped in the production route table with no cap and no deadline
confirmed.detail:
`handleStreamProbe` is registered unconditionally in `buildMux` (/var/home/glw907/Projects/dubplate/internal/serve/serve.go:188) and is described in its own doc comment as existing "solely to prove ... that cloudflared delivers bytes incrementally" for gate 1 (serve.go:428-439). STATUS records gates 1-2 as already PASSED, so this endpoint's purpose is served, yet it stays in the production surface.

As written it is a resource sink. It clears the write deadline (`rc.SetWriteDeadline(time.Time{})`, serve.go:458), then loops on a 15s ticker with no maximum duration, no concurrent-stream cap per identity, and no global cap (serve.go:478-490). The only exit is client disconnect or shutdown. Each open stream pins a goroutine, a connection, and a `*http.Server` conn slot indefinitely. Any single on-roster caller can open thousands with a trivial script and exhaust the process; because it is a CORS-simple POST with no body requirements (see the CSRF finding), a cross-site page can open them from a victim's browser too.

It also carries the unbounded `Last-Event-ID` -> `strconv.Atoi` reflection at serve.go:448-452, harmless on its own but more attack surface than a retired probe should have.
confirmed.fix: Delete the route now that gate 1 has passed; the handler can stay in the tree behind a build tag or a config flag if it is wanted for a future re-measurement. If it must ship, bound it: a hard max stream duration, a per-identity concurrent-stream limit, and an overall cap.

CONFIRMED — I could not refute it; every code claim checks out, and one of them is stronger than the reviewer stated.

- serve.go:448-452 — the `Last-Event-ID` → `strconv.Atoi` reflection is there as described (bounded by `Atoi`, harmless on its own, exactly as the finding characterizes it).

It does not. `http.Server` calls `connReader.startBackgroundRead` once the request body hits EOF (`$GOROOT/src/net/http/server.go:2124-2126`), and that function clears the read deadline (`server.go:741`).
